status_reasoning: Reviewers acknowledge Ybx1 binds sqt RNA but express concern about specificity, noting Ybx1 is 'a fairly ubiquitous sequence-nonspecific RNA binding protein' with 'apparent ability to bind nucleic acids with little specificity.' They request 'quantitative binding assays that demonstrate specificity' to distinguish this from Ybx1's 'long and checkered history' of non-specific binding.

Reviewers directly challenge the translational repression mechanism, stating 'there is no convincing direct evidence in this manuscript that Ybx1 really does regulate squint mRNA translation.' They request 'evidence regarding the mechanism for how Ybx1 inhibits translation' and note contradictory literature showing 'Ybx1 promoting rather than repressing translation in cancer cells.'

Reviewers find the splicing/polyadenylation observations 'intriguing' but question the interpretation, noting 'evidence for cytoplasmic splicing is at best debatable' and that 'data provided in the manuscript are also compatible with a role of Ybx1 in transcription.' They request 'evidence supporting the mechanisms by which Ybx1 suppresses splicing of sqt RNA in the cytoplasm.'

Reviewers challenge the interpretation of the mutant phenotype, stating 'the phenotype can also be interpreted as a defect in late cytokinesis during early embryogenesis, leading to an aberrant ectopic syncytium' rather than YSL expansion. They note that 'the possibility that these defects are simply a cause of an aberrant syncytium due to defects in early cytokinesis is not well substantiated' and request the 'crucial and absolutely critical experiment' of a Mybx1/MZoep double mutant.

Reviewers acknowledge the bead implantation experiments but note they 'do not preclude' the alternative possibility that 'targets other than nodal are also misregulated, resulting in defects in cell division.' The experiments provide some support for Nodal involvement but do not definitively rule out other mechanisms.

Reviewers identify mRNA transport defects as 'the most apparent early defect' and question whether 'this is the primary phenotype, rather than the proposed precocious translation.' They note that 'Wnt8a transport can also be affected' and ask whether 'the defect mostly affects ooplasmic transcripts that need to be transported to the forming blastodisc,' questioning the specificity to sqt.

Reviewers question whether control mRNAs 'encompass all known pathways of mRNA localization, in particular those transported animally through axial streaming,' suggesting the specificity controls may be incomplete. This relates to their concern about whether the phenotype is specific to sqt or affects multiple transcripts.

While reviewers acknowledge elevated Nodal signaling in mutants, they question whether this is the primary cause of phenotypes or whether 'targets other than nodal are also misregulated, resulting in defects in cell division.' They emphasize that without the Mybx1/MZoep double mutant, the specificity of Nodal's role remains uncertain.

Reviewers do not explicitly discuss the rescue experiments with lefty or sqt mutant backgrounds. However, their insistence on the 'crucial and absolutely critical' Mybx1/MZoep double mutant suggests they view the existing genetic evidence as insufficient to conclusively demonstrate that Nodal signaling is the sole cause of the phenotypes.

Reviewers fundamentally challenge the main conclusions, stating the work is 'too preliminary' and that 'additional experimental evidence would need to be provided.' They argue the study 'will not go beyond the many other papers on Ybx1 and will just be another description of Ybx1 binding to RNA' without more direct mechanistic evidence and the critical double mutant experiment.
